steps.title: In the ground

form.name: Zinc concentrate
form.label: tens to hundreds of grams of indium a tonne

steps.text: Indium has no ore of its own. It occurs in sphalerite, the main zinc mineral, at tens to a few hundred grams a tonne, and in some tin and copper ores. It is recovered only as a by-product.

steps.title: Ride with zinc
steps.text: Zinc ore is mined and floated, and the concentrate goes to a smelter. As the zinc is roasted and leached, indium collects in the dusts and residues. Only smelters with an indium circuit catch it; the rest lose it to waste.
steps.india: Indian zinc smelters report no indium recovery.

steps.title: Extract
steps.text: The residue is leached with acid, and solvent extraction pulls out the indium. It is then precipitated onto zinc or aluminium plates as a spongy metal, a step called cementation.

steps.title: Refine
steps.text: The sponge is melted, cast into anodes and electrorefined. Vacuum distillation and zone refining take it further for semiconductors.

steps.title: Make
steps.text: Most indium is oxidised, mixed with one part in ten of tin oxide, and pressed and fired into ceramic tiles of indium tin oxide (ITO). These are the targets from which a thin film is sputtered onto glass.

steps.title: Use
steps.text: ITO is the rare material that is both transparent and electrically conductive, so it forms the invisible electrodes of every flat screen and touch panel. Indium also goes into solders, into thin-film solar cells and into indium phosphide chips for fibre networks.
steps.india: Display and electronics demand, all imported.

steps.title: Recycle
steps.text: Sputtering puts only about a third of a target onto the glass. The rest, the spent target and the coating on the chamber walls, is collected and refined again, mostly in Japan, South Korea and China. Indium in old screens is rarely recovered.
steps.india: CSIR-NML has a laboratory process that recovers indium from scrap LCD panels.
